Senior Portraits

This shoot is about you.

It’s About You

This shoot is meant to highlight your personality, your interests, and the details that make you, you. I consider this a collaborative process — so let’s work together to make some photographs that you’ll enjoy for years to come.

That means I want to know things before we shoot. What you’ve spent the last four years doing. What you’re walking into next. Whether you’d rather be on a trail, downtown, or standing in the field behind your house. Whether you love being photographed or have been dreading this since your mom booked it. All of that changes how I shoot you, and none of it is a wrong answer.

What I’m after is a set of photographs that look like you at eighteen — not a stiffer, more posed version of you, and not the same session everyone in your class is getting.

Bring Your Whole Life Into It

This is the part people forget and always love afterward. Bring the things that are actually yours. Your instrument. Your ball, your bat, your cleats. The letterman jacket. Your camera, your truck, your horse, your dog. A stack of books for whatever you’re studying next year.

Four years of your life are worth having in a frame, and the props are never really props — they are the reason you’ll still recognise yourself in these photographs in twenty years. If you’re not sure whether something will work, bring it anyway and we’ll figure it out together.

Same with where we go. Your field, your gym, the pier, the trail you run, downtown, the place you and your friends have been going since freshman year. If somewhere means something to you, that is a better location than anywhere I could pick for you.

The Next Chapter

This is a huge milestone in your life and it deserves to be documented and remembered. These photographs will serve as a great reminder of your accomplishments and the person you have become through your journey so far.

And they get used more than you expect. The announcement. The yearbook. The wall at your grandparents’ house. The frame your mom keeps on her desk long after you’ve moved out. This is the last time your family photographs you as someone who lives at home, and that turns out to matter to them more than anybody says out loud at the time.

About me

It’s my goal to make photographs that tell your story.

My name is Mike Thezier (pronounced: tee-zee-ey) — my last name looks nothing like it sounds. I am a film and digital photographer based in Southern California. I love the outdoors, traveling, coffee, a good movie, but most of all sharing in those experiences with others.

I shoot both digital and actual film, and I’ve been photographing seniors long enough to know that the ones who say they are bad at this are usually the ones who end up with my favourite frames. You don’t need to know how to pose and you don’t need to be someone who loves the camera. That part is my job.

I enjoy working with my clients to create images that are genuine and compelling — and I’d rather spend an hour finding out who you are than an hour arranging you.

The experience

Before the day

Once you’re booked we’ll talk before we shoot — where you want to go, what you want to bring, and what you’re going to wear. I’ll send you my full what-to-wear guide, but the short version is this: bring clothes you already own and already feel like yourself in. Two or three looks with some variety — one dressier, one everyday, and if you bring a third, make it the one that’s most you.

Bring your cap, gown and tassel, and anything else you earned along the way — stole, cords, medals, a decorated cap. Pull the gown out of the bag a few days early and steam it, or hang it in the bathroom during a hot shower. They come creased and it shows.

If your school colours are part of the plan, tell me beforehand so the gown and your outfits work together instead of fighting each other. These are the details that take five minutes to sort out in advance and cannot be fixed afterwards.

The session itself

We meet on location, usually in the last couple of hours before sunset when the light is worth having. The first ten minutes are the awkward ones — that is true of almost everybody, and I plan for it. We start easy, walking and talking, and you forget the camera is there sooner than you expect.

You don’t have to know how to pose. I’ll direct you when you need it and leave you alone when you don’t. If you hate being photographed, tell me that up front and we’ll work around it — some of my favourite frames come from the moments between the ones people think are the picture.

We change looks as we go and work the location for what it gives us. And we’ll grab a proper set with the cap and gown on even if you’re not sure you want them. You’ll be glad you have those.

Bring a friend or a parent if you want one there. Some seniors are more themselves with someone they know behind me, and some would rather it was just the two of us. Either is completely normal — just tell me which one you are.

Your gallery

Your gallery lands in your inbox two to three weeks after the session, and that first scroll through it is the part I actually do this for. Full resolution, downloadable, yours to keep, print and share — no watermarks, no per-image fees, and no waiting on prints to find out what you got.

You can hand the yearbook one straight to your school, put your favourite on the announcement, and send the whole gallery to your grandparents in one link. From there, prints, books, albums and wall pieces are available whenever you want them. Nothing expires on you.

When to shoot

Most seniors shoot in the fall, ahead of yearbook deadlines, or in the spring once the weather turns and cap and gown have arrived. Both work. What doesn’t work is leaving it until the week the yearbook is due, when the only slots left are whatever nobody else wanted.

If you have a hard date — a yearbook deadline, announcements that need to go out, a grandparent visiting — tell me what it is when you get in touch and we’ll work backward from it. I’ll tell you honestly whether I can make it rather than find out together afterwards.

Fall books up first, and I take a limited number of senior sessions each season so that nobody gets a rushed one. If you already know roughly when you want to shoot, the date is the part worth locking in early — everything else we can decide later.

Full Session

1.5 hours

The Keepsake

$1,250

Built for a family who wants something to hand down, not just a folder of files.

Prints & Products. Every session includes the full resolution downloads. From your gallery you’ll have prints, books, albums and other products available at any time — The Keepsake simply builds the album in from the start, designed with you rather than ordered on your own.

Questions

I’m not photogenic. Really.
Almost everybody says this, and almost nobody is right. What people usually mean is that they don’t know what to do with their hands and they hate being watched. Both of those are my job, not yours. I’ll give you something to do rather than a pose to hold, and we’ll keep moving until you forget I’m there.
When should we shoot?
Fall, ahead of yearbook deadlines, or spring once cap and gown have arrived. If you have a deadline, tell me the date and we’ll work back from it.
Where do we shoot?
On location, and wherever possible somewhere that means something to you — your field, your barn, downtown, the trail you run. I’m based in the Temecula Valley and shoot across Southern California. Orange County, San Diego and the coast are all regular trips and carry no separate travel fee at these rates.
What do I wear?
Clothes you already own and feel like yourself in. Two to three looks with some variety, plus your cap and gown and anything you earned. I’ll send you the full guide once you’re booked and we’ll go over it together before the day.
Can my family or my dog come?
Yes, and I’d encourage it. A few frames with your parents and siblings are almost always the ones that end up on the wall at home — and your dog has earned a spot as much as anyone. Just bring them along.
How long until I see them?
Your gallery arrives two to three weeks after we shoot. If you have a hard deadline, say so when you book and I’ll tell you honestly whether I can make it.

Next step

Pick the session that fits and send it to me with your name, your school, and roughly when you’re hoping to shoot. I’ll come back with dates that work.

A 50% retainer holds your date and comes off the total; the balance is due on the day of your session. I’ll send the contract and the invoice through HoneyBook, so it’s signed and paid in one place. Until the retainer is in, the date stays open to whoever asks next.

If you’re still deciding, send me a message anyway and tell me what you’re thinking. I’d rather answer a question now than have you book the wrong session.
